extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art criticism, art historians, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-aesthetic criteria for evaluating Renaissance sculpture and Michelangelo's poetry, focusing on expression, form, style, and emotional temperament. Emphasises qualities such as inwardness, studied incompleteness, balance of strength and sweetness, and the evocation of life and pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality and intensity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should bring what was inward to the surface, be concerned with individual expression, individual character and feeling, and the special history of the special soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater emphasizes that art worth doing shows the special, inward life of persons rather than a mere outward or general life. Example: fifteenth-century Tuscan sculptors' 'studied sepulchral portraits of particular persons' that convey repose and sacred grace. Anti-pattern: work that sacrifices personal feeling to generalized form or decor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of too-hard realism (avoid caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a too hard realism which tends to harden into caricature in the representation of feeling in sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Michelangelo and others soften realism to prevent expressions of feeling becoming caricature. Guidance: relieve hard realism by suggestion, incompleteness, or subtle finish; anti-pattern: overworked literalism that becomes grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied incompleteness as method (suggestion over full realization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving sculpture in a puzzling sort of incompleteness which suggests rather than realises actual form; this incompleteness acts as Michelangelo's equivalent for colour and etherealises pure form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater treats deliberate partial finish as an artistic device that communicates breath, pulsation, and life, asking the spectator to 'complete' the half-emergent form. Example: the rough-hewn/ delicately finished juxtaposition in Michelangelo's works and the retained morsel of uncut stone on David. Scoring note: incompleteness is not sloppiness but intentional finish; anti-pattern: accidental roughness or unfinished work that lacks expressive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine passion/intensity with yielding, flexible life
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the utmost amount of passion and intensity with a sense of a yielding and flexible life to secure both vitality and a wonderful force of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal work balances fervour with a responsive, living quality—producing force without rigidity. Example: Michelangelo's ability to blend intensity with 'a yielding and flexible life.' Anti-pattern: intensity that hardens into static or maniacal energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conventionalism and low relief to harmonise expression and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a system of conventionalism—subduing curves that indicate solid form and throwing the whole into lower relief—to unite tranquillity and intense individual expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tuscan sculptors (e.g., Luca della Robbia) combine select elements of pure form with studied incompleteness and low relief to avoid hard realism while preserving expression. Practical guidance: in relief work, simplify or subdue modelling to maintain serenity without losing expressive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate, restrained use of colour in applied art
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce colour thoughtfully into humbler media (pottery) to bring new grace, but exercise restraint—especially in representing flesh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luca della Robbia used bright colours for pottery frames and garlands, often keeping flesh uncoloured and reserving blues/whites for sacred figures. Guidance: adopt colours 'subdued a little' and appropriate to medium and subject; anti-pattern: garish or anatomically coloured flesh in ceramics when tradition and effect call for restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: The impress of a personal quality (intimité)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should bear the seal of an artist's inward mood and original apprehension—an unmistakable personal expressiveness or intimité.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater treats this as rare but decisive: the 'impress of a personal quality' is what makes imaginative works truly valuable. Example: fifteenth-century artists whose work feels near and original. Scoring note: originality of temperament and expressive signature are prized over mere technical virtuosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strangeness must be sweet (balance surprise with pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should excite or surprise us, but the strangeness must be 'sweet'—a lovely strangeness that gives pleasure as well as astonishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater argues that while a certain strangeness is indispensable, it must accompany charm; anti-pattern: strength or oddity that repels without delight (monstrous or forbidding in inferior hands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic self-sufficiency (avoid dependence on accessories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The charm and sweetness of a work should not depend on external accessories or mere embellishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike writers who rely on incidental 'lovely accidents' (butterfly on barricade), Michelangelo's sweetness is inherent in his work. Guidance: ensure the artwork's core conception carries its own appeal; anti-pattern: reliance on external motifs or props to make the main idea palatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on creation/penetrative suggestion of life (human centrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceive art as an act of creating life—especially the human form—bringing life out of inert material with a sense of resurrection or animation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater notes Michelangelo's preoccupation with creating man as a primary artistic act (e.g., Creation of Adam, Resurrection motifs). Guidance: emphasise animation and inner life over mere decorative natural scenery; anti-pattern: empty landscape detail that substitutes for the core human presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve traces of material and process (connection to source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain traces of the material or the quarry—unfinished bits or roughness—to keep a vital connection between the work and its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 'morsel of uncut stone' remaining on David to maintain connexion with the place whence it was hewn; such traces can intensify the sense of life emerging from stone. Anti-pattern: over-polishing that removes tactile evidence of material and making the work feel disconnected from its source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce both pleasure and charm alongside surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Works must not only surprise but also give pleasure and exert a charm over the viewer; both are indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater states that excitement without pleasure is insufficient. Evaluate art for its capacity to combine novelty with agreeable impact. Anti-pattern: shocking works that lack aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with death as dignifying and serious
rubrics_metrics.description: A preoccupation with death, seriously and humanely presented, can dignify work and be a mark of high quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Florentine tradition treats thoughts of death as ennobling; Pater links solemnity about mortality to depth and distinction in art (e.g., tomb sculptures, funerary imagery). Anti-pattern: flippant or sensational treatment of death that undermines dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke compassion/pity (Pietà) over divinised sorrow
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest moral sentiment in some great art is human pity—an almost 'hopeless, rayless, almost heathen sorrow'—rather than a triumphant or doctrinally divine grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Michelangelo's recurring subject is the Pietà and maternal pity; guidance: aim for raw human compassion and tender realism in sorrow, not merely symbolic or stylised religious triumph. Anti-pattern: sentimentalised or schematic sorrow lacking tactile human anguish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatricality; balance strength with temperate sweetness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid theatricality and an overemphasis on raw strength without the tempering element of sweetness; disciples who love strength alone produce theatrical effects foreign to the master's gravitas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater criticizes followers who mimic Michelangelo's strength but miss his 'grave and temperate sweetness', yielding theatricality. Practical implication: model emotional force with restraint and depth; anti-pattern: grandiloquent poses and gestures that lack inward conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: In poetry: temper vehement emotions by idealising them (calm, meditative sweetness)
rubrics_metrics.description: In lyric poetry, strong emotions should be tranquillised by idealising and inwardly refining them into a prevailing tone of calm and meditative sweetness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater describes Michelangelo's sonnets as bringing passionate thought under control by recording them (similar to Goethe's response)—the poems are 'a calm and meditative sweetness' where distress remains only as a trace. Guidance: in composing passionate verse, seek idealisation and serenity rather than ungoverned complaint; anti-pattern: poems that are merely plaintive without inward refinement.
